value: Like entries in a lighthouse keeper’s logbook: each one is dated, but most aren’t about any one passing ship.
reason: A ship’s log is kept per voyage, so the example suggests the opposite of the point: a log need not belong to any one request.

value: Pulling is how Prometheus normally collects data: the server decides when to scrape each target. The Overview lists “time series collection happens via a pull model over HTTP” among its main features.
reason: The old sentence reverses cause and effect and calls pull a ‘default’, which the source does not say.

value: Name two advantages that Prometheus’s FAQ gives for pulling metrics rather than pushing them.
reason: The FAQ lists three advantages; ‘what two advantages’ implies there are exactly two.

value: The FAQ judges pulling only slightly better than pushing overall, and says it should not be a major point when choosing a monitoring system.
reason: The FAQ gives no ‘main’ reason; it ranks nothing and adds that the choice is not a major point.

value: With pulling, each target serves its own metrics over HTTP, so a person can open that same endpoint in a browser, just as Prometheus does when it scrapes.
reason: The old reasoning tied browser inspection to Prometheus reaching out; it is the target’s own HTTP endpoint that makes it possible.

value: No. Once the job has exited there is nothing left to scrape. If it is a service-level batch job, not tied to one machine, this is the case the Pushgateway is meant for.
reason: The Pushgateway page limits its valid use to service-level batch jobs; a machine-tied batch job should use the textfile collector.

value: The job has to hand over its result before it exits. For a batch job tied to one machine, the docs recommend the Node Exporter’s textfile collector instead of the Pushgateway.
reason: Keeps the card consistent with machine-batch-job-uses-textfile and the source’s ‘Alternative strategies’.

value: A service-level job’s metrics carry no machine or instance label, so they don’t go stale when a machine is renamed or removed. That matters because the Pushgateway never forgets pushed series unless they are deleted by hand.
reason: The single-point-of-failure risk comes from monitoring many instances through one Pushgateway, not from other use cases; and it never forgets series whatever the job type.

value: Metrics are numeric data aggregated over time. Logs are timestamped messages, not necessarily tied to a request. Traces record one request’s path, built from spans.
reason: Source says logs ‘aren’t necessarily associated with’ a request; ‘not tied to a request’ drops the hedge.

value: OpenTelemetry documentation, Observability primer
reason: The metric definition is under ‘Reliability and metrics’, not ‘Understanding distributed tracing’; cite the whole page.

value: https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/observability-primer/
reason: Matches the new source line, which spans two sections.

value: In OpenTelemetry’s observability primer, what question does reliability answer?
reason: The primer names no ‘common mistake’ and never speaks of measuring from the inside.

value: “Is the service doing what users expect it to be doing?”
reason: Verbatim from the primer (tier B).

value: So a system can be up 100% of the time and still be unreliable, if what it does while it is up isn’t what users expect.
reason: Paraphrase of the primer’s own sentence.

value: This is the primer’s own example for reliability: being up is not the same as doing what users expect.
reason: The primer uses the black-shoes example to define reliability, not to explain how to choose an SLI.

value: The primer’s example of an SLI is the speed at which a web page loads: something users experience directly.
reason: The claim about system-centric SLIs looking healthy is not in the source.

value: The way reliability is communicated to the organisation and other teams, by attaching one or more SLIs to business value.
reason: Source says ‘business value’ and ‘organization/other teams’; ‘business-meaningful target’ changes the wording’s meaning.

value: Besides a name and start and end timestamps, an OpenTelemetry span can carry {{c1::span events}}: structured log messages that mark single points in time during the span.
reason: The source list also has parent span ID, span links and span status, so the old cloze had several right answers.

value: A span also holds a span context, attributes, span links, a span status and, unless it is the root span, a parent span ID.
reason: Gives the full list from the Traces page, so the card no longer implies five items.

value: “Synchronous” here doesn’t mean blocking code or async/await; it means the call is made now, not queued for later processing.
reason: The source says ‘synchronous’ ‘does not refer to async/await’; ‘the caller is waiting on this call right now’ says the opposite.

value: Its parent is always a producer span, even though the consumer span may start long after the producer span has ended.
reason: The source says the parent of a consumer span is always a producer, so they are parent and child, not ‘linked rather than nested’.

value: A service logs key=value lines such as level=ERROR service=user-authentication userId=12345 message="Failed login attempt", and other services log different keys, with no shared schema. What kind of log is this?
reason: One line cannot show whether the schema is stable; the difference from a structured log must be in the front.

value: An unstructured log: it has no consistent structure, so parsing it at scale takes extra work, such as regular expressions and custom parsers.
reason: Source needs ‘a regular expression to parse their timestamps and custom parsers’ for the bodies.

value: The primer says logs become far more useful when they are part of a span, or correlated with a trace and a span: that link, not the log text, supplies the missing context.
reason: ‘OpenTelemetry correlates logs with spans where it can’ is not in the source.

value: For a span that tracks adding an item to a shopping cart, attributes might record the user’s ID, the item’s ID and the cart ID.
reason: ‘What make a span searchable and filterable’ is not in the source; this example is.

value: It’s a generic interface: any tool that can write target lists to files can feed Prometheus, which is how custom service discovery mechanisms plug in.
reason: Source: ‘serves as an interface to plug in custom service discovery mechanisms’; ‘almost any’ overstates.

value: If a container declares no ports, the pod role still creates a target for it without a port, so a port can be added by hand through relabeling.
reason: ‘So one can be added’ is unclear: ‘one’ reads as a target, but it means a port.

value: Besides static_configs, name two service discovery mechanisms that Prometheus’s configuration reference lists for finding scrape targets.
reason: The reference lists some thirty mechanisms, so ‘what two other ways’ has many right answers.

value: Any two of many: for example, file-based service discovery and Kubernetes service discovery. The reference also lists DNS, Consul and several cloud providers.
reason: Matches the new front.

value: A contract with users, written or implied, that sets out what happens when the service meets or misses the SLOs inside it.
reason: Tier C source: the old back copied the book’s sentence almost word for word.

value: A quick test: ask what follows if the SLOs are missed. If nothing explicit does, it is almost certainly an SLO, not an SLA.
reason: The book says ‘almost certainly’; ‘means it is an SLO’ drops the hedge.

value: Like a gym membership that refunds a month’s fee if the pool is closed for more than a week: the pool’s opening promise is the SLO, and the refund is what makes it an SLA.
reason: The old courier/refund example gives away refund-clause-is-sla word for word.

value: Explicit consequences for meeting or missing the SLOs. Financial ones, such as a rebate or a penalty, are the easiest to spot.
reason: Tier C: reworded away from the book’s sentence.

value: The book notes that people often say “SLA” when they mean an SLO; a so-called SLA violation is usually just a missed objective.
reason: ‘Almost certainly’ is the book’s wording for the consequence test, not for what people call an SLA; the footnote says ‘Most people really mean SLO’.

value: Ask what happens if the SLOs are missed. If nothing explicit follows, it is almost certainly an SLO; an explicit consequence, such as a penalty, points to an SLA.
reason: Restores the book’s hedge ‘almost certainly’.

value: Most people say “SLA” when they mean an SLO. A real SLA breach is a contract matter that could end up in court.
reason: ‘Which is rare’ is not in the source; wording moved further from the tier C footnote.

value: A team commits to “checkout pages load in under 2 seconds for 99% of visits”, with no refund or penalty if they miss it. Is this best described as an SLO or an SLA?
reason: Tier C: the old scenario (average search latency under 100 milliseconds) is the book’s own example.

value: An SLO: a target for a measured service level, with none of the contractual consequences an SLA would add.
reason: Moves away from the book’s ‘target value … for a service level’ wording.
